title: Morning and evening protection
hookLine: in the name of Allah, with whose name nothing harms, three times (Abu Dawud; Tirmidhi)
tomorrow: what does it mean to be 'pleased' with God, out loud?

cards: Lock the door, check the stove, check the lock again: the small ritual at the edge of the day that says, let nothing happen tonight.
The Prophet ﷺ gave one, said three times in the morning and three in the evening: bismillahil-ladhi la yadurru ma'a ismihi shay'.
In the name of Allah, with whose name nothing on earth or in the sky can harm, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. So, one question for today: can words keep you safe?

teach.b: The hadith, in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, comes from Uthman ibn Affan: whoever says it three times in the evening won't be struck by a sudden affliction until morning, and three times in the morning, until evening.
Then comes the most human detail in the report, and it's worth telling someone tonight. The man passing it on, Uthman's son Aban, was later struck by a partial paralysis, and someone stared at him.
Aban said: the hadith is as I told you, but on that day I was angry, and I forgot to say it. He didn't hide the hard case. He told it inside the hadith.
So the tradition's answer isn't a charm. The line begins with a name, bismillah, and puts the day under that name. Now a neighbor who keeps the same two edges.

teach.h: THE SHEMA: LYING DOWN, RISING UP.
teach.b: In Jewish tradition, the Shema is said evening and morning, following the Torah's words about speaking God's words, in the JPS translation, "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."
Two traditions, the same two edges of the day, the same instinct to begin and end with God.

And one honest difference: the Shema's words come from the Torah itself and declare that God is one; this Muslim line comes from the Prophet's sayings and asks for protection, counted out three times.
Neither has to be the other.

how: Muslims who keep the morning and evening remembrances (adhkar) say this line three times after the dawn prayer and again in the evening.

games.q: what does “morning and evening protection” mean?
o: a line said at dawn and dusk, under God's name
a prayer said only during a storm or danger
a verse hung over the door to guard a house

games.q: two edges, two traditions — tap the pairs.
p: forgot it the day he was struck
said lying down and rising up

s: the hadith's narrator hid the time it seemed not to work
Aban told it himself: he had been angry and forgot to say it that day.
Jewish tradition also keeps words for evening and morning
the Shema, following the Torah: when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
the Shema and this line are the same prayer in two languages
the Shema comes from the Torah and declares God is one; this line asks for protection.

games.q: your roommate asks: 'so is your three-times line just like the Shema?' what's the honest, kind answer?
o: yes, exactly the same; every bedtime prayer says one thing.
alike in timing and in starting with God; different in source and in words.
not at all; there's nothing in common between them.
games.why: both keep the edges of the day; the Shema is Torah declaring God one, the Muslim line is a saying of the Prophet ﷺ asking protection.

practice: Say the line three times, aloud and slowly, in Arabic or in English: in the name of Allah, with whose name nothing on earth or in the sky can harm, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
If you don't pray, sit instead with the question underneath it: what am I handing over tonight that I can't guard myself? Let the quiet hold the answer.

wordCard.voice: Morning and evening protection: a line from the Prophet's sayings, said three times at each edge of the day, putting the day under God's name.

orig.note: Arabic: in the name of Allah, the words the line begins with.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: nothing harms with his name, at edges of the day more than one tradition keeps. Two remembrances in.

sources.ref: Sunan Abu Dawud 5088; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3388 (narrated by Uthman ibn Affan)
